newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Anti-Taleban alliance hopes to regain mutineers.
newsitem.headline: Anti-Taleban alliance hopes to regain mutineers.

text.p: The main northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif was calm on Thursday as the anti-Taleban alliance holding it said it was more confident it would win back mutineers who had caused tensions.

People bustled through dusty streets and there were few outward signs of worries that this stronghold of opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum might be vulnerable to an emerging alliance between renegade foreign minister General Abdul Malik and the purist Taleban Islamic militia.
"Nothing is happening here," alliance foreign ministry protocol director Mohammad Ayub told reporters confidently. "But everything is different," he added.

An alliance spokesman told Reuters in Kabul by satellite telephone that he was more confident that Malik, who apparently mutinied on Monday to join the Taleban, could be persuaded to return to the alliance.
"Today the negotiations went better, Malik sent some elders to see Dostum. I am more confident than last night," opposition spokesman Dr Abdullah said.
In Mazar-i-Sharif, a U.N. plane left for the Pakistani capital Islamabad with aid workers not permanently based in the city, which is the capital of Balkh province.

Sub-office head of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Cesar Dubon, said U.N. agencies had suspended all activities in the north because of uncertainty and difficulties in gaining acess to some areas where they operated.
However, U.N. officials said there were no immediate plans for a full-scale evacuation.

At least eight Soviet-made helicopters, a few MiG fighters and two civilian airliners of Dostum's Balkh Airlines were parked at the dilapidated Mazar-i-Sharif airport. But soldiers guarding it did not seem to be on a heightened state of alert.
The alliance said Malik had mutinied in protest against Dostum rather than in support of the Taleban.
The alliance was thrown into disarray and its frontline crumbled when Malik, pivotal in the defence against the Taleban as Faryab province governor turned against Dostum on Monday.
But uncertainty remained as to how much territory the Taleban took and how much was still under opposition control.
Abdullah said there had been no clashes between Malik's and Dostum's forces on the front line close to the border of Jawzjan and Faryab provinces.
"There were no clashes on the front line today and that is a good sign," he said.

The Taleban, which controls Kabul and more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, says Malik and his forces have been absorbed into its ranks and that the whole of Faryab and Sar-i-Pul provinces were under their control.

Taleban forces and those of Hezb-i-Wahadat, a mainly Shi'ite group in the opposition alliance, were battling on Wednesday night in the district of Sheikh Ali, close to the strategic Shiber Pass in central Afghanistan, Abdullah said.
The pass leads into the Bamiyan valley and from there to the north of the country.

"Last night the Taleban attacked in Sheikh Ali, but their attack was pushed back. They took some losses and retreated." he said. The Taleban were unavailable for comment on the situation in Sheikh Ali.
